fatal_errors: The proposed method is spark plasma sintering, whereas the target method is liquid-metal dealloying by immersion of directionally segregated WTaVTi in molten Cu.
The starting material is incorrectly reconstructed as a powder blend rather than an as-cast, single-BCC WTaVTi alloy with W/Ta-rich dendrites and sacrificial Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
The hypothesis omits the selective Ti–Cu exchange mechanism, retention of W/Ta/V-rich ligaments, and formation of the W-rich passivating interlayer that stabilizes the RHEA/Cu interface.

The claim that rapid processing suppresses detrimental interdiffusion does not explain the target structure, which requires extensive millimeter-scale Cu penetration and selective replacement over 96 hours.
No evidence supports the asserted improvements in mechanical or irradiation performance, and composite mechanical strength was not directly demonstrated in the target study.
explanation: The response recognizes the general incompatibility challenge between refractory alloys and Cu, but reconstructs neither the method nor the governing mechanism. The target uses liquid-metal dealloying at 1200 °C for 96 h to selectively replace Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels with Cu, producing aligned bicontinuous Cu channels and RHEA ligaments stabilized by an approximately 300 nm W-rich interlayer. SPS, powder consolidation, rapid cooling, and suppression of interdiffusion are unrelated to those central findings. The proposed SPS-versus-conventional-sintering experiment is somewhat falsifiable, but it does not test selective dealloying, interfacial passivation, directional transport, or the target thermal and helium-irradiation outcomes. With no cited evidence and several unsupported performance claims, the alternative is not sufficiently substantiated to count as a plausible alternative.
